sections.title: Two systems, one coordinated body

board_events.text: Why does a body need coordination at all?
Every organ must work in step with the others.
NEURAL SYSTEM: rapid, point-to-point control using electrical impulses carried by nerve cells.
ENDOCRINE SYSTEM: slower, longer-lasting control using chemical hormones.

board_events.text: Neural = fast and targeted. Endocrine = slow and broadcast.
Together they keep the body's internal environment stable.
The endocrine system is the next chapter. This chapter takes the neural half.

segments.text: <curious> Your heart, your gut, your muscles, your glands — why do they never work at cross purposes?
Because every organ must work in step with the others. That does not happen by accident. The body achieves it through two systems.
First, the neural system: rapid, point to point control, using electrical impulses carried by nerve cells. Point to point — a nerve runs from a definite source to a definite target, like a wire.
Second, the endocrine system: slower, longer lasting control, using chemical hormones. A hormone is poured into the blood and travels everywhere — a broadcast, not a wire.
Side by side, the division of labour is obvious. Electrical, fast, one target, brief effect — that is neural. Chemical, slower, whole body, longer lasting — that is endocrine.
So: neural is fast and targeted, endocrine is slow and broadcast. Neither is better. They are built for different jobs.
Together they keep the body's internal environment stable. That stability is the point — everything else here is machinery serving it.
Endocrine is your next chapter. This one takes the neural half, and starts by zooming in on the cell that makes rapid signalling possible.
<curious> आपका heart, gut, muscles, glands — ये सब कभी एक दूसरे के खिलाफ काम क्यों नहीं करते?
क्योंकि हर organ को बाकी सबके साथ step में काम करना ही है। ये अपने आप नहीं होता। Body इसे दो systems से achieve करती है।
पहला, neural system: rapid, point to point control, nerve cells के electrical impulses से। Point to point — nerve एक definite source से definite target तक जाती है, एक wire की तरह।
दूसरा, endocrine system: slower, longer lasting control, chemical hormones से। Hormone blood में डाला जाता है और हर जगह पहुँचता है — broadcast, wire नहीं।
दोनों साथ रखिए तो division of labour साफ़ है। Electrical, तेज़, एक target, brief effect — ये neural। Chemical, धीमा, पूरी body, longer lasting — ये endocrine।
तो: neural fast और targeted, endocrine slow और broadcast। कोई better नहीं। दोनों अलग jobs के लिए बने हैं।
साथ मिलकर ये body का internal environment stable रखते हैं। यही असली मकसद है — बाकी सारी machinery इसी की service में है।
Endocrine आपका अगला chapter है। ये वाला neural half लेता है, और शुरू होता है उस cell पर zoom करके जो rapid signalling possible बनाती है।

sections.title: Nerve net to nerve cord: organisation across animals

board_events.text: Neural organisation across animals
The neural system becomes more elaborate as animals become more complex.
Cnidarians (e.g. Hydra): a diffuse NERVE NET of loosely connected neurons. No brain, no central control.
Higher invertebrates (insects, earthworm, cockroach): a definite BRAIN plus segmental GANGLIA linked by nerve cords.
Vertebrates, including humans: a large BRAIN, a SPINAL CORD, and nerves reaching every part of the body.

board_events.text: The trend is increasing CENTRALISATION: no controller → local controllers → one command centre.
A nerve net still works. What it cannot do is decide.

segments.text: Before we open the human system, see where it came from. Nervous systems are not built alike across the animal kingdom.
The rule runs one way: the neural system becomes more elaborate as animals become more complex. A complicated body demands complicated wiring.
Start simple, with the cnidarians — Hydra is your book's example. Hydra has a diffuse nerve net: neurons loosely connected, spread through the body. No brain. No central control anywhere.

Step up to higher invertebrates — insects, earthworm, cockroach. Now a definite brain, plus segmental ganglia, which are clusters of nerve cell bodies, linked by nerve cords. Control has begun to gather.
Step up again to vertebrates, ourselves included: a large brain, a spinal cord, and an extensive network of nerves reaching every part of the body.
Lay the three side by side and the story tells itself. A scattered net with nobody in charge. Then a brain, with ganglia repeating down the body. Then one brain, a cord, and nerves everywhere.
The trend deserves a name: centralisation. From no controller, to local controllers, to a single command centre with the body wired into it.
<chuckle> But note what this does not mean. Poke a Hydra and it responds perfectly well. A nerve net works. What it cannot do is decide. Centralisation buys judgement, not reaction.
Human system खोलने से पहले देखिए ये आया कहाँ से। Animal kingdom में nervous systems एक जैसे नहीं बने होते।
Rule एक ही तरफ़ चलता है: जैसे-जैसे animals complex होते हैं, neural system elaborate होता जाता है। Complicated body को complicated wiring चाहिए।
Simple से शुरू — cnidarians, और आपकी book का example है Hydra। Hydra में diffuse nerve net होता है: neurons loosely connected, body में फैले हुए। कोई brain नहीं। कहीं central control नहीं।
अब higher invertebrates — insects, earthworm, cockroach। यहाँ definite brain, plus segmental ganglia, यानी nerve cell bodies के clusters, nerve cords से जुड़े हुए। Control इकट्ठा होने लगा है।
एक step और ऊपर, vertebrates, हम खुद भी: एक बड़ा brain, एक spinal cord, और nerves का extensive network जो body के हर हिस्से तक पहुँचता है।
तीनों साथ रखिए तो कहानी खुद बोलती है। बिखरा net, कोई in charge नहीं। फिर brain, और body में repeat होते ganglia। फिर एक brain, एक cord, और हर तरफ़ nerves।
इस trend का एक नाम बनता है: centralisation। कोई controller नहीं, से local controllers, और फिर एक single command centre जिससे पूरी body wired है।
<chuckle> पर ध्यान दीजिए इसका मतलब क्या नहीं है। Hydra को छेड़िए, वो respond बढ़िया करता है। Nerve net काम करता है। वो decide नहीं कर सकता। Centralisation judgement देता है, reaction नहीं।

sections.title: The human plan: central and peripheral

board_events.text: The human neural system at a glance
Just TWO parts. Everything in this chapter sits inside one of them.
CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) = brain + spinal cord. Where information is received, processed, and acted upon.
PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (PNS) = all the nerves branching out from the CNS.
PNS traffic runs both ways: AFFERENT fibres carry sensory information IN; EFFERENT fibres carry motor commands OUT to muscles and glands.

Next: zoom in on the neuron, the cell that makes all of this possible.

segments.text: Now the human system. The good news: the top level map is not complicated at all.
It divides into just two parts. Two. Every structure named in this chapter — every nerve, every ganglion, every brain region — sits in one of them, and knowing which is half the battle in exams.
First, the central nervous system, the C N S: exactly two organs, the brain and the spinal cord. Information is received here, processed here, acted upon here. The decisions happen here.
Second, the peripheral nervous system, the P N S: all the nerves branching out from the C N S. It does not decide anything. It carries.
And it carries both ways. Afferent fibres carry sensory information inward, to the C N S. Efferent fibres carry motor commands outward, to muscles and glands. Information in, commands out.
The tree makes membership explicit. Neural system splits into central and peripheral. Central into brain and spinal cord. Peripheral into afferent and efferent fibres.

<whisper> Here is the trap the paper setter loves. Asked which of these is C N S, students reach for anything that sounds important. Only brain and spinal cord. Every nerve and ganglion outside them is peripheral.
That is the map. Now we do the opposite of zooming out — all the way in, to the cell that makes every bit of this possible.
अब human system। अच्छी बात: top level map बिलकुल complicated नहीं है।
ये सिर्फ़ दो हिस्सों में बँटता है। दो। इस chapter का हर structure — हर nerve, हर ganglion, हर brain region — इन्हीं में से एक में बैठता है, और कौन-से में, ये जानना exam की आधी लड़ाई है।
पहला, central nervous system, यानी C N S: exactly दो organs, brain और spinal cord। Information यहीं receive होती है, यहीं process होती है, यहीं act किया जाता है। Decisions यहीं होते हैं।
दूसरा, peripheral nervous system, यानी P N S: वो सारी nerves जो C N S से निकलकर फैलती हैं। ये कुछ decide नहीं करता। ये carry करता है।
और दोनों directions में carry करता है। Afferent fibres sensory information अंदर, C N S तक लाती हैं। Efferent fibres motor commands बाहर, muscles और glands तक ले जाती हैं।
Tree membership साफ़ कर देता है। Neural system बँटा central और peripheral में। Central बँटा brain और spinal cord में। Peripheral बँटा afferent और efferent fibres में।

<whisper> अब वो trap जो paper setter को पसंद है। पूछा जाए कि C N S क्या है, तो students कुछ भी important-sounding चुन लेते हैं। सिर्फ़ brain और spinal cord। उनके बाहर की हर nerve और ganglion peripheral है।
ये रहा map। अब zoom out का उल्टा — बिलकुल अंदर तक, उस cell तक जो ये सब possible बनाती है।

sections.title: The signalling problem: a message that must not garble

board_events.text: A pinprick on the toe must become 'pull your foot back' in a fraction of a second
You would not shout the message across the whole distance. You would pass it station to station, along a dedicated line.
The NEURON is the cell that carries the message.
Its long, wire-like AXON is the line the message travels along.

board_events.text: Built for one-way, long-distance signalling: DENDRITES receive, AXON carries away, SYNAPTIC KNOBS hand over.
The neuron is the structural AND functional unit of the nervous system.
But here is the twist: nothing actually races down the wire.

segments.text: <curious> Imagine the Indian Railways at its busiest. A message — train delayed at Itarsi — must cross the country, fast, without getting garbled.
You would not shout it across the distance. You would pass it station to station, along a dedicated line, each station handing on a clean copy.
Your body faces the same problem, smaller. A pinprick on your toe must become a pull your foot back command in a fraction of a second. The cell carrying it is the neuron.
And the line it travels along is the neuron's long, wire-like axon. Hold both: the neuron is the carrier, the axon is the line. Everything else hangs on that frame.
Look at the layout. Trouble at one end, a dedicated line with stations along it, a command at the other — all inside a fraction of a second.
The neuron's shape follows the job. Short branched dendrites to receive signals. A single long axon to carry the impulse away. Synaptic knobs at the tip to hand it to the next cell.

That is why the neuron is called the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Structural, because it is the building block. Functional, because it is the smallest thing that can do the job.
But now the twist — the one that makes biology cleverer than the railways. Nothing actually races down that wire. Not a chemical, not a particle. Let us see what really happens.
<curious> Indian Railways को सबसे busy time पर सोचिए। एक message — Itarsi पर train delayed — पूरे देश को पार करना है, तेज़ी से, बिना garble हुए।
आप इसे चिल्ला कर नहीं भेजेंगे। आप इसे station to station pass करेंगे, एक dedicated line पर, हर station एक clean copy आगे देते हुए।
आपकी body के सामने यही problem है, छोटे scale पर। पैर की उंगली पर pinprick को एक second के हिस्से में pull your foot back वाला command बनना है। इसे carry करने वाली cell है neuron।
और जिस line पर ये चलता है वो है neuron का लंबा, wire जैसा axon। दोनों पकड़िए: neuron carrier है, axon line है। बाकी सब इसी frame पर टँगा है।
Layout देखिए। एक सिरे पर trouble, बीच में stations वाली dedicated line, दूसरे सिरे पर command — और ये सब एक second के हिस्से में।
Neuron की shape उसके job के हिसाब से है। छोटे branched dendrites, signals receive करने को। एक single लंबा axon, impulse को दूर ले जाने को। सिरे पर synaptic knobs, अगली cell को सौंपने को।
इसीलिए neuron को nervous system की structural और functional unit कहते हैं। Structural, क्योंकि ये building block है। Functional, क्योंकि ये सबसे छोटी चीज़ है जो काम कर सकती है।
पर अब twist — वही जो biology को railways से clever बनाता है। उस wire पर असल में कुछ दौड़ता ही नहीं। न chemical, न particle। देखते हैं होता क्या है।

sections.title: Nothing travels: the impulse regenerates itself

board_events.text: The twist that makes biology cleverer than the railways
A neuron does NOT physically send a substance racing down the wire.
The message is ELECTRICAL: a fleeting flip in the voltage across the neuron's membrane.
It REGENERATES ITSELF at every point along the way.
Like a line of dominoes toppling. Or a stadium wave — no single person runs round the ground, but the wave races all the way round.

board_events.text: At rest, the membrane is a tightly stretched BOWSTRING: loaded, more positive outside, more negative inside. This state is POLARISED.
A stimulus is the finger that plucks the string. It snaps — the voltage briefly reverses — and that snap pulls the next bit of string out of place, which snaps in turn.
The 'snap' travelling down the axon IS the nerve impulse. The neuron re-loads the string behind the wave.

segments.text: So if the message is not a train, what is it? Here the railway picture breaks.
A neuron does not send a substance racing down the wire the way a train moves down a track. Nothing is dispatched at one end and delivered at the other. That intuition has to go.
Instead the message is electrical — a fleeting flip in the voltage across the neuron's membrane. That flip is the whole message.
And it regenerates itself at every point along the way. It is not weakening and being pushed along. It is recreated, fresh, over and over.
Two pictures land this. A line of dominoes: no domino travels, but the toppling races along. Or the stadium wave — nobody runs round the ground, yet the wave circles it.
Look at the panels. Dominoes toppling. The axon, with a flip at one patch and the rest still waiting. And underneath, the bowstring — because that is what the resting membrane is.
Picture the resting membrane as a tightly stretched bowstring. Loaded with potential energy. More positive outside, more negative inside. Use the name precisely: this state is polarised.
A stimulus is the finger that plucks the string. It snaps — the voltage briefly reverses — and that snap pulls the next bit out of place, which snaps in turn. And so on, down the line.
The snap travelling down the axon is the nerve impulse. And behind the wave, the neuron re-loads the string, ready for the next message.
तो अगर message train नहीं है, तो है क्या? यहीं railway वाली picture टूटती है — अच्छे से।
Neuron कोई substance wire पर उस तरह नहीं दौड़ाता जैसे train track पर। एक सिरे से भेजा और दूसरे पर deliver हुआ — ऐसा नहीं होता। ये intuition छोड़ दीजिए।
इसकी जगह message electrical है — membrane के आर-पार voltage में एक fleeting flip। अंदर-बाहर के charge के फ़र्क़ में brief change। यही flip पूरा message है।
और ये रास्ते के हर point पर खुद को regenerate करता है। ये कमज़ोर होकर धकेला नहीं जा रहा। ये बार-बार, ताज़ा, फिर से बनता है — पूरे रास्ते।
दो pictures से बात बैठती है। Dominoes की line: कोई domino travel नहीं करता, पर गिरना दौड़ता है। या stadium wave — कोई ground का चक्कर नहीं लगाता, फिर भी wave पूरा चक्कर लगाती है।
Panels देखिए। गिरते dominoes। Axon, एक patch पर flip और बाकी इंतज़ार में। और नीचे bowstring — क्योंकि resting membrane यही है।
Resting membrane को कसी हुई bowstring की तरह देखिए। Potential energy से loaded। बाहर ज़्यादा positive, अंदर ज़्यादा negative। नाम precisely use कीजिए: ये state polarised है।
Stimulus वो उंगली है जो string को pluck करती है। String snap करती है — voltage थोड़ी देर reverse होता है — और वो snap अगले हिस्से को खींच देता है, जो अपनी बारी में snap करता है।
Axon पर दौड़ता यही snap nerve impulse है। यही definition है, एक picture में। और wave के पीछे neuron string को फिर load कर देता है, अगले message के लिए तैयार।

sections.title: The fine print: what the neat picture assumes

board_events.text: Limiting conditions — and exams love the exceptions
The 'loaded bowstring' resting state is NOT passive. It costs continuous energy (ATP).
Stop the energy supply and the gradient runs down. No impulse is possible.
An impulse is ALL-OR-NONE: a stimulus either crosses the threshold and fires a full impulse, or nothing happens.

board_events.text: A 'stronger' pinch does not make a 'bigger' impulse. It makes impulses fire MORE OFTEN.
Conduction is UNIDIRECTIONAL at a chemical synapse: dendrite → cell body → axon → next cell.
Though an isolated axon can technically conduct both ways if stimulated in the middle.

segments.text: That picture is neat. Neat pictures have fine print, and here the fine print is where the marks are. Four conditions.
First: the loaded bowstring resting state is not passive. It costs continuous energy — specifically A T P, spent every second of every day.
And that has a hard consequence. Stop the energy supply and the gradient runs down. The string un-loads. No impulse is possible. A neuron that cannot pay cannot fire.
Second, tested constantly: an impulse is all or none. A stimulus either crosses threshold and fires a full impulse, or nothing happens. There is no half impulse.

Read the graph across. Weak stimulus, nothing. Below threshold, still nothing. Cross threshold — a full spike. Stimulate harder — the same full spike. Harder still — the spikes simply come more often.
So say it precisely: a stronger pinch does not make a bigger impulse. It makes impulses fire more often. Intensity is coded as frequency, not size. That sentence answers a whole family of questions.
Third: conduction is unidirectional at a chemical synapse. Dendrite, cell body, axon, next cell. One way — and later we will see which machinery enforces it.
But note your book's honest caveat: an isolated axon can technically conduct both ways if stimulated in the middle. The one-way rule comes from the synapse, not the axon.
Fourth: the model assumes an intact membrane with working ion channels. Damage the myelin, as in demyelinating disease, and conduction slows or fails.
Picture साफ़-सुथरी है। पर साफ़ pictures के साथ fine print आता है, और marks उसी में हैं। चार conditions।
पहली: loaded bowstring वाली resting state passive नहीं है। चुप बैठना free नहीं है। इसमें लगातार energy लगती है — specifically A T P, हर दिन हर second।
और इसका सख़्त नतीजा है। Energy supply रोकिए और gradient run down हो जाता है। String un-load हो जाती है। कोई impulse possible नहीं। जो neuron pay नहीं कर सकता, वो fire नहीं कर सकता।
दूसरी, लगातार test होती है: impulse all or none है। Stimulus या तो threshold cross करके पूरा impulse fire करता है, या कुछ नहीं होता। आधा impulse नहीं होता।
Graph पढ़िए। Weak stimulus — कुछ नहीं। Threshold से नीचे — फिर भी कुछ नहीं। Threshold cross — पूरा spike। ज़ोर से — वही पूरा spike। और ज़ोर से — spikes बस ज़्यादा बार आते हैं।
तो precisely कहिए: तेज़ चिकोटी बड़ा impulse नहीं बनाती। वो impulses ज़्यादा बार fire कराती है। Intensity frequency में code होती है, size में नहीं। यही sentence questions के पूरे family का जवाब है।
तीसरी: chemical synapse पर conduction unidirectional है। Dendrite, cell body, axon, अगली cell। एक तरफ़ — और आगे देखेंगे कौन-सी machinery इसे enforce करती है।
पर book का honest caveat नोट कीजिए: isolated axon technically दोनों तरफ़ conduct कर सकता है, अगर बीच में stimulate करें। One-way rule synapse से आता है, axon से नहीं।

चौथी: model मानता है कि membrane intact है और ion channels काम कर रहे हैं। Myelin damage हो, जैसे demyelinating disease में, तो conduction धीमा या fail हो जाता है। Picture उतनी ही अच्छी जितना hardware।

sections.title: The neuron: three regions, one direction

board_events.text: The neuron (nerve cell)
A microscopic, EXCITABLE cell specialised to receive, conduct, and transmit impulses. It has three regions.
CELL BODY (cyton / soma / perikaryon): contains the nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and Nissl's granules.
DENDRITES: short, branched processes arising from the cell body. They conduct impulses TOWARDS the cyton.
AXON: a single, long process arising from the AXON HILLOCK. It conducts impulses AWAY from the cyton.
The axon ends in branched axon terminals, tipped with SYNAPTIC KNOBS — which contain synaptic vesicles with neurotransmitters.

board_events.text: Mnemonic: Axon = Away. Dendrite = Deliver-in.
Three regions, three names each worth knowing — cyton, soma, and perikaryon all mean the cell body.

segments.text: Now the anatomy. The neuron is a microscopic, excitable cell, specialised to receive, conduct, and transmit impulses. Excitable is load-bearing — it can be triggered into that voltage flip.
It has three regions. Get these and their directions right and a large chunk of this chapter is yours.
First, the cell body — three names, all fair game: cyton, soma, or perikaryon. It contains the nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and Nissl's granules. This is the office of the cell.
Second, the dendrites: short, branched processes arising from the cell body. Their direction is fixed — they conduct impulses towards the cyton. They are the receiving end.
Third, the axon: a single, long process arising from the axon hillock. Note single — many dendrites, only ever one axon. And its direction is the opposite: away from the cyton.
The axon ends in branched axon terminals, tipped with synaptic knobs. Inside those knobs sit synaptic vesicles holding neurotransmitters — the chemicals that hand the message to the next cell.
Trace it in one sweep: dendrites in, cyton with nucleus and Nissl's granules, the hillock, the long myelinated axon with its nodes, the terminals, the knobs.
And the mnemonic that saves you under pressure: Axon equals Away. Dendrite equals Deliver-in. Two words, and the most swapped fact in the chapter stops being swappable.
One caution. Cyton, soma, and perikaryon are the same structure. A question calling it a perikaryon is not testing new content — it is testing whether the vocabulary rattles you.

अब anatomy। Neuron एक microscopic, excitable cell है, जो impulses receive, conduct और transmit करने के लिए specialised है। Excitable load-bearing शब्द है — इसे voltage flip में trigger किया जा सकता है।
इसके तीन regions हैं। बस तीन। ये और इनकी directions सही कर लीजिए, तो chapter का बड़ा हिस्सा आपका है।
पहला, cell body — तीन नाम, तीनों paper में आ सकते हैं: cyton, soma, perikaryon। इसमें nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, और Nissl's granules होते हैं। ये cell का office है।
दूसरा, dendrites: cell body से निकलते छोटे, branched processes। इनकी direction fixed है — ये impulses cyton की तरफ़ conduct करते हैं। ये receiving end हैं।
तीसरा, axon: एक single, लंबा process जो axon hillock से निकलता है। Single नोट कीजिए — dendrites कई, axon हमेशा एक। और direction उल्टी: cyton से दूर।
Axon branched axon terminals में ख़त्म होता है, जिनके सिरों पर synaptic knobs हैं। उनके अंदर synaptic vesicles, जिनमें neurotransmitters — वो chemicals जो message अगली cell को सौंपते हैं।
एक sweep में trace कीजिए: dendrites अंदर, cyton nucleus और Nissl's granules के साथ, hillock, लंबा myelinated axon nodes के साथ, terminals, knobs। यही cell है।
और वो mnemonic जो pressure में बचाता है: Axon यानी Away। Dendrite यानी Deliver-in। दो शब्द, और chapter का सबसे swap होने वाला fact swap होना बंद।
नामों पर एक चेतावनी। Cyton, soma, perikaryon एक ही structure हैं। Question उसे perikaryon कहे तो वो नया content test नहीं कर रहा — वो देख रहा है कि vocabulary से आप घबराते हैं या नहीं।

NISSL'S GRANULES: masses of rough endoplasmic reticulum (with ribosomes) that synthesise proteins.
Present in the CYTON and DENDRITES. Absent in the AXON and AXON HILLOCK.

board_events.text: A classic NEET fact. Factories are in the office (cyton + dendrites), not on the highway (axon).
NEUROGLIA (glial cells): non-conducting supporting cells that protect and nourish neurons.
They make up MORE THAN HALF the volume of neural tissue.
AXOPLASM: the cytoplasm inside the axon. It carries mitochondria and microtubules — but no Nissl's granules.
Mitochondria DO occur in the axon. That is exactly why they fail the 'absent in axon' test.

segments.text: Three terms now, each a whole question in its own right. Do not skim these.
Nissl's granules. Chemical nature first: masses of rough endoplasmic reticulum, carrying ribosomes. And because ribosomes make protein, the function follows — protein synthesis for the neuron.
Now the distribution, and this is what gets tested. Present in the cyton and the dendrites. Absent in the axon, and absent in the axon hillock too. Two places present, two absent.
See it drawn. Granules through the cell body, granules in the dendrites, and along the whole axon — nothing. That contrast is the examinable fact.
Your book calls this a classic N E E T fact, and the picture that locks it in: the factories are in the office — cyton and dendrites — not on the highway, which is the axon.
Second term: neuroglia, or glial cells. Non-conducting supporting cells that protect and nourish neurons. Non-conducting is key — they do not carry impulses.
<excited> And the statistic that surprises everyone: neuroglia make up more than half the volume of neural tissue. More than half. The neurons get the glory, outweighed by their own support staff.
Third: axoplasm — the cytoplasm inside the axon. It carries mitochondria and microtubules. But no Nissl's granules. The axon has an interior; it just has no protein factory in it.
And that sets the classic trap. Mitochondria do occur in the axon. Answer mitochondria to a question about something absent from the axon, and you fail the test it was setting.
अब तीन terms, और हर एक अपने आप में पूरा question बन चुकी है। इन्हें skim मत कीजिए।

Nissl's granules। पहले chemical nature: rough endoplasmic reticulum के masses, जिन पर ribosomes हैं। और चूँकि ribosomes protein बनाते हैं, function निकल आता है — ये neuron के लिए proteins synthesise करते हैं।
अब distribution, और यही test होता है। Present cyton में और dendrites में। Absent axon में, और axon hillock में भी। दो जगह present, दो जगह absent।
Drawing देखिए। Cell body में granules, dendrites में granules, और पूरे axon पर — कुछ नहीं। Cross लगा हुआ। यही contrast examinable fact है।
Book इसे classic N E E T fact कहती है, और lock करने वाली picture: factories office में हैं — cyton और dendrites — highway पर नहीं, और highway है axon।
दूसरी term: neuroglia, या glial cells। Non-conducting supporting cells। ये neurons को protect और nourish करती हैं। Non-conducting key है — ये impulses carry नहीं करतीं। ये neurons को ज़िंदा रखती हैं।
<excited> और वो statistic जो सबको चौंकाती है: neuroglia neural tissue के आधे से ज़्यादा volume बनाती हैं। आधे से ज़्यादा। Glory neurons को, पर वज़न में उनका अपना support staff भारी।
तीसरी: axoplasm — axon के अंदर का cytoplasm। इसमें mitochondria और microtubules हैं। पर Nissl's granules नहीं। Axon का interior है; बस उसमें protein factory नहीं।
और यही classic trap set करती है। Mitochondria axon में होते हैं। Axon से absent किसी चीज़ के question में mitochondria लिखा, तो आप वही test fail कर गए जो वो ले रहा था।

board_events.text: Types of neurons — classified by NUMBER OF PROCESSES
MULTIPOLAR: 1 axon + 2 or more dendrites. Typically found in the cerebral cortex; motor neurons.
BIPOLAR: 1 axon + 1 dendrite. Typically found in the retina of the eye; olfactory epithelium.
UNIPOLAR: cell body with a single process. Usually the embryonic stage.

board_events.text: Count the processes FIRST, then name the type. Never the other way round.
'Polar' means the poles — the processes coming off the cell body. Multi, bi, uni.
This is classification by SHAPE. A separate classification, by JOB, comes next.

segments.text: Neurons are not all the same shape. The first classification your book gives is purely structural: by the number of processes coming off the cell body.
Multipolar. One axon plus two or more dendrites — many poles. Found in the cerebral cortex, and motor neurons are multipolar too. This is the shape you probably picture when you hear neuron.
Bipolar. One axon plus one dendrite — two poles, one at each end. Remember the retina of the eye, and the olfactory epithelium, the smell-sensing lining of the nose.
Unipolar. A cell body with a single process — one pole. And here the location is not a place but a stage: your book says unipolar neurons occur usually in the embryonic stage.
Look at the three side by side and naming stops being vocabulary and becomes counting. Many processes. Two processes. One process. That is the entire classification.
So the rule: count the processes first, then name the type. Never the other way round. Students who recall the name first end up guessing; students who count read the answer off the picture.
It helps that polar means the poles — the processes coming off the cell body. Multi, bi, uni: many, two, one. The word is telling you the answer if you listen.
And keep one boundary clear. This classification is by shape. A completely separate classification, by job — by what the neuron does — comes next.
Neurons सब एक shape के नहीं। Book की पहली classification पूरी structural है: cell body से निकलते processes की संख्या से।
Multipolar। एक axon plus दो या ज़्यादा dendrites — कई poles। Cerebral cortex में मिलते हैं, और motor neurons भी multipolar हैं। Neuron सुनकर शायद यही shape दिमाग़ में आती है।
Bipolar। एक axon plus एक dendrite — दो poles, हर सिरे पर एक। याद रखिए retina of the eye, और olfactory epithelium, नाक की smell-sensing lining।
Unipolar। Cell body के साथ एक process — एक pole। और यहाँ location जगह नहीं, एक stage है: book कहती है unipolar neurons usually embryonic stage में होते हैं।
तीनों साथ देखिए तो naming vocabulary नहीं, counting बन जाती है। कई processes। दो processes। एक process। बस यही पूरी classification है।
तो rule: पहले processes गिनिए, फिर type का नाम लीजिए। कभी उल्टा नहीं। जो पहले नाम याद करते हैं वो guess करते हैं; जो गिनते हैं वो picture से answer पढ़ लेते हैं।
मदद ये करती है कि polar मतलब poles — cell body से निकलते processes। Multi, bi, uni: कई, दो, एक। शब्द खुद answer बता रहा है, बस सुनिए।
और एक boundary साफ़ रखिए। ये classification shape से है। एक बिलकुल अलग classification job से — neuron करता क्या है — अब आ रही है।

sections.title: Myelinated vs non-myelinated fibres

board_events.text: Myelinated vs non-myelinated fibres
MYELINATED: the axon is wrapped by SCHWANN CELLS, which form a multilayered, fatty, insulating MYELIN SHEATH.
Gaps between successive sheaths are the NODES OF RANVIER, where the membrane is exposed.
Found in spinal and cranial nerves.
NON-MYELINATED: the axon is enclosed by a Schwann cell, but NO myelin sheath is formed.
Common in the autonomic and somatic neural systems.

board_events.text: NEURILEMMA: the outer plasma-membrane layer of the Schwann cell, surrounding the sheath.
At the node of Ranvier the myelin is discontinuous. The neurilemma may be continuous.

segments.text: Now a distinction that will matter enormously when we talk about speed. Nerve fibres come in two kinds: myelinated and non-myelinated.

In a myelinated fibre the axon is wrapped by Schwann cells, which form a multilayered, fatty, insulating myelin sheath around it. Fatty and insulating — remember both, because insulation is the point.
But the sheath is not one continuous tube. Gaps between successive sheaths are the nodes of Ranvier. At a node the membrane is exposed. Bare.
Where are myelinated fibres found? Your book is specific: spinal and cranial nerves. Tie location to type — match-the-column questions do exactly that.
In a non-myelinated fibre something subtler happens. The axon is still enclosed by a Schwann cell — the cell is there — but no myelin sheath is formed. Schwann cell present, myelin absent.
And these are common in the autonomic and somatic neural systems. So: myelinated goes with spinal and cranial nerves; non-myelinated with autonomic and somatic.
Put the two fibres one above the other. Above: a beaded chain of sheaths with bare nodes between. Below: a plain covered axon, no sheath, no nodes at all. No nodes is the giveaway.
One more term: the neurilemma. The outer plasma-membrane layer of the Schwann cell, surrounding the sheath. Easy to skip, easy to test.

<whisper> And the subtle line most students never notice. At the node of Ranvier the myelin is discontinuous — that is the whole idea of a node. But the neurilemma may be continuous. Two layers, two answers.
अब एक distinction जो कुछ मिनटों में बहुत काम आएगा, जब speed की बात होगी। Nerve fibres दो तरह की: myelinated और non-myelinated।
Myelinated fibre में axon को Schwann cells लपेटती हैं, जो उसके चारों तरफ़ multilayered, fatty, insulating myelin sheath बनाती हैं। Fatty और insulating — दोनों याद, क्योंकि insulation ही point है।
पर sheath एक continuous tube नहीं। लगातार sheaths के बीच gaps होते हैं, और वही gaps nodes of Ranvier हैं। Node पर membrane exposed होती है। नंगी।
Myelinated fibres कहाँ? Book specific है: spinal और cranial nerves में। Location को type से बाँधिए, क्योंकि match the column यही करता है।
Non-myelinated fibre में subtle बात होती है। Axon को Schwann cell फिर भी घेरती है — cell मौजूद है — पर myelin sheath बनती नहीं। Schwann cell present, myelin absent।
और ये common हैं autonomic और somatic neural systems में। तो: myelinated के साथ spinal और cranial nerves; non-myelinated के साथ autonomic और somatic।
दोनों fibres एक के ऊपर एक रखिए। ऊपर: sheaths की माला, बीच में नंगे nodes। नीचे: सादा ढका axon, न sheath न node। Nodes का न होना ही पहचान है।
एक और term: neurilemma। Schwann cell की बाहरी plasma-membrane layer, जो sheath को घेरती है। Skip करना आसान, question बनाना भी आसान — एक पल दीजिए।
<whisper> और वो बारीक line जो ज़्यादातर students देखते ही नहीं। Node of Ranvier पर myelin discontinuous होता है — node का मतलब ही यही है। पर neurilemma continuous हो सकता है। दो layers, दो answers।

sections.title: Afferent, efferent, interneuron: classification by job

board_events.text: Functional classification — by job, not by shape
The same three-part hardware is wired into three functional roles.
AFFERENT (sensory) neurons: carry impulses from a receptor / sense organ TOWARDS the CNS — they bring information IN, via the dorsal root.
EFFERENT (motor) neurons: carry impulses FROM the CNS to an EFFECTOR — a muscle or a gland. They send commands OUT.
INTERNEURONS (association neurons): lie WITHIN the CNS and link afferent to efferent neurons.

This afferent–interneuron–efferent chain is exactly the wiring reused in the reflex arc.

segments.text: We have classified neurons by shape. Now by job. And notice: the hardware does not change. The same three-part cell is wired into three roles.

Afferent neurons, also called sensory. They carry impulses from a receptor or sense organ towards the central nervous system. They bring information in. And your book adds: they enter via the dorsal root.
Efferent neurons, also called motor. They carry impulses from the C N S out to an effector — a muscle or a gland. Afferent brings the report; efferent carries the order.
Interneurons, also called association neurons. These lie within the C N S, and link afferent to efferent. They are the middle of the chain — the part that connects the in to the out.
See the chain in one line. Receptor on the left. Afferent neuron running in. Interneuron inside the dashed box, which is the C N S. Efferent neuron running out. Effector on the right.
Your book gives a frame worth saying out loud until it sticks: afferent Arrives at the brain; efferent Exits to the effector. The first letter tells you the direction.
It works because A and E are exactly the letters students confuse. Attach A to Arrives and E to Exits, and the two words stop being noise and start carrying meaning.
And hold on to this chain. This exact afferent, interneuron, efferent sequence is the wiring you will reuse whole when you reach the reflex arc at the end of this chapter.
हमने neurons को shape से classify किया। अब job से — वो करते क्या हैं। और notice कीजिए: hardware बदलता नहीं। वही three-part cell तीन roles में wire होती है।
Afferent neurons, यानी sensory। ये impulses receptor या sense organ से central nervous system की तरफ़ ले जाते हैं। ये information अंदर लाते हैं। Book जोड़ती है: ये dorsal root से enter करते हैं।
Efferent neurons, यानी motor। ये impulses C N S से बाहर effector तक ले जाते हैं — muscle या gland। Afferent report लाता है; efferent order ले जाता है।
Interneurons, यानी association neurons। ये C N S के अंदर होते हैं, और afferent को efferent से जोड़ते हैं। ये chain का बीच हैं — जो in को out से connect करता है।
Chain एक line में देखिए। बाएँ receptor। अंदर आता afferent neuron। Dashed box के अंदर interneuron, और वो box है C N S। बाहर जाता efferent neuron। दाएँ effector।
Book एक frame देती है, इसे ज़ोर से बोलिए जब तक चिपक न जाए: afferent Arrives at the brain; efferent Exits to the effector। पहला letter direction बता रहा है।
ये इसलिए काम करता है क्योंकि A और E वही letters हैं जो students confuse करते हैं। A को Arrives से, E को Exits से जोड़िए, और दोनों शब्द शोर की जगह meaning बन जाते हैं।
और इस chain को पकड़े रखिए। यही afferent, interneuron, efferent वाला sequence आप पूरा दोबारा use करेंगे जब chapter के आख़िर में reflex arc तक पहुँचेंगे।

sections.title: The resting membrane: polarised at about minus seventy millivolts

board_events.text: The resting (polarised) membrane
When a neuron is NOT conducting an impulse, its axonal membrane is POLARISED: positive outside, negative inside.
A steady voltage of about -70 mV.
Factor 1 — SELECTIVE PERMEABILITY. At rest the membrane is comparatively permeable to K+, nearly impermeable to Na+, and impermeable to the large negatively-charged proteins trapped in the axoplasm.

board_events.text: INSIDE (axoplasm): high K+, large trapped negatively-charged proteins, only a little Na+.
OUTSIDE (extracellular fluid): the mirror image — rich in Na+, poor in K+.
K+ trickles OUT far more readily than Na+ comes IN — and the proteins can never leave at all.
So the inside settles at a net negative charge. That is the polarised state.

segments.text: Now we open the bowstring and see what it is made of. Two factors set up the resting state; this section takes the first.
Start with the fact. When a neuron is not conducting an impulse, its axonal membrane is polarised: positive outside, negative inside. That is resting, stated as a charge arrangement.
And it holds a steady voltage of about minus seventy milli volts. The minus sign is not decoration — it tells you the inside is the negative side. Read the sign as a direction.

Factor one is selective permeability. At rest the membrane is comparatively permeable to potassium, nearly impermeable to sodium, and impermeable to the large negatively charged proteins trapped in the axoplasm.
The diagram makes the compartments concrete. Read it as two facing shelves, with the membrane between them.
Inside, in the axoplasm: a high concentration of potassium, plus those large trapped negatively charged proteins, and only a little sodium.
Outside, in the extracellular fluid: the mirror image — rich in sodium, poor in potassium. Whatever the inside has a lot of, the outside has little of.
Now put permeability together with distribution, and the voltage falls out. The membrane lets potassium trickle out far more readily than sodium in. And the proteins, being negative, can never leave.
So positive charge leaks out, negative charge is stuck in, and the inside settles at a net negative charge. That is not a rule to memorise. That is a consequence — the polarised state.
अब bowstring खोलकर देखते हैं वो बनी किस चीज़ से है। Resting state को दो factors set up करते हैं; ये section पहला लेता है।
Fact से शुरू। जब neuron impulse conduct नहीं कर रहा, तब उसकी axonal membrane polarised है: बाहर positive, अंदर negative। यही resting है, charge arrangement की भाषा में।
और इसमें steady voltage है, लगभग minus सत्तर milli volts। Minus का चिह्न सजावट नहीं — वो बता रहा है negative side अंदर है। चिह्न को direction की तरह पढ़िए।

पहला factor है selective permeability। Rest पर membrane potassium के लिए comparatively permeable, sodium के लिए nearly impermeable, और axoplasm में फँसे बड़े negatively charged proteins के लिए impermeable है।
Diagram compartments concrete कर देता है। इसे दो आमने-सामने shelves की तरह पढ़िए, बीच में membrane।
अंदर, axoplasm में: potassium की high concentration, plus वो बड़े फँसे negatively charged proteins, और sodium बस थोड़ा।
बाहर, extracellular fluid में: उल्टी तस्वीर — sodium से भरपूर, potassium में कमज़ोर। जो अंदर ज़्यादा, वो बाहर कम।

अब permeability और distribution साथ रखिए, voltage खुद निकल आता है। Membrane potassium को बाहर कहीं आसानी से रिसने देती है, बनिस्बत sodium को अंदर आने देने के। और proteins, negative होने से, कभी बाहर जा नहीं सकते।
तो positive charge बाहर रिसता है, negative अंदर फँसा रहता है, और अंदर net negative charge बैठ जाता है। ये रटने वाला rule नहीं। ये नतीजा है — polarised state।

sections.title: The sodium-potassium pump: paying for the gradient

board_events.text: Factor 2 — the sodium-potassium pump
An ATP-driven pump that expels 3 Na+ OUT for every 2 K+ IN.
It works AGAINST the concentration gradient.

board_events.text: The result: high Na+ outside, high K+ and proteins inside — an ionic imbalance that STORES energy.
This is the loaded bowstring, made concrete.
The pump's continuous 3:2 export prevents the hard-won gradient from running down.
So 'resting' is not rest. It is continuous, ATP-funded work.

segments.text: Selective permeability explains why charge separates. But if potassium keeps leaking out and sodium trickling in, the gradient should die. Something must keep paying. That is factor two.
The sodium potassium pump. It is A T P driven, and its stoichiometry is one of the most reliably examined numbers here: it expels three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in.

And crucially, it works against the concentration gradient — pushing sodium into a region already full of sodium, pulling potassium into one already full of potassium. Uphill both ways. That is why it costs A T P.
Watch the arrows. Three sodium ions forced out of the axoplasm. Two potassium ions hauled in. And the pump in the membrane, spending A T P every moment to do it.
The result is the distribution we just met: high sodium outside, high potassium and proteins inside. An imbalance. And an imbalance held away from equilibrium stores energy.
Which is the bowstring, made concrete. The stored energy is real, it sits in that ion gradient, and the impulse will spend it when the moment comes.
So the pump's continuous three to two export prevents the hard-won gradient from running down. It does not set the gradient up once and walk away. It holds it, against a constant leak, forever.

<whisper> And that reframes the word resting. Resting is not rest. A resting neuron does continuous, A T P funded work just to stay ready — which is exactly why cutting the energy supply abolishes the impulse.

Selective permeability बताती है charge अलग क्यों होता है। पर एक problem खड़ी होती है: अगर potassium रिसता रहे और sodium आता रहे, तो gradient ख़त्म हो जाना चाहिए। किसी को क़ीमत चुकानी है। वो है factor दो।
Sodium potassium pump। ये A T P driven है — energy जलाता है — और इसकी stoichiometry यहाँ के सबसे भरोसेमंद examinable numbers में है: हर दो potassium अंदर लाने के बदले तीन sodium बाहर फेंकता है।
और अहम बात, ये concentration gradient के ख़िलाफ़ काम करता है। Sodium को वहाँ धकेलना जहाँ sodium भरा है, potassium को वहाँ खींचना जहाँ potassium भरा है। दोनों तरफ़ चढ़ाई। इसीलिए A T P लगता है।
Arrows देखिए। तीन sodium ions axoplasm से बाहर धकेले जा रहे। दो potassium ions अंदर खींचे जा रहे। और pump membrane में, हर पल A T P ख़र्च करता हुआ।
नतीजा वही distribution: बाहर high sodium, अंदर high potassium और proteins। एक imbalance। और equilibrium से दूर रखा imbalance energy store करता है।
यही bowstring है, concrete बनी। Stored energy असली है, वो उसी ion gradient में है, और वक़्त आने पर impulse उसी को ख़र्च करेगा।
तो pump का लगातार three to two export मेहनत से बने gradient को run down होने से रोकता है। वो gradient एक बार बनाकर चला नहीं जाता। वो उसे थामे रखता है, लगातार leak के ख़िलाफ़, हमेशा।
<whisper> और इससे resting शब्द का मतलब बदल जाता है। Resting मतलब आराम नहीं। Resting neuron सिर्फ़ तैयार रहने के लिए लगातार A T P funded काम करता है — इसीलिए energy काटते ही impulse ख़त्म हो जाता है।

sections.title: The action potential, step one: depolarisation

board_events.text: The action potential — step 1: depolarisation
A stimulus that reaches THRESHOLD triggers a rapid, self-regenerating voltage change at that site.
The membrane at the stimulated point suddenly becomes far more permeable to Na+.
Na+ rushes IN. The inside becomes positive and the outside negative — the polarity REVERSES.
To roughly +30 mV.

board_events.text: This reversed state IS the action potential.
The logic: only a cation moving INWARD can make the inside positive.
The membrane was already holding Na+ outside. Open the gates, and the gradient does the rest.

segments.text: The string is loaded. Now somebody plucks it. A stimulus that reaches threshold triggers a rapid, self regenerating voltage change at that site — and only at that site, for now.
What changes is permeability. The membrane at the stimulated point becomes far more permeable to sodium. That is the switch being thrown. Everything after is consequence.
Because remember what was waiting outside. Sodium, in quantity, held out by a membrane that barely let it in, and pulled by a negative interior. Open that gate and sodium rushes in.
In it comes, carrying positive charge, until the inside becomes positive and the outside negative. The polarity reverses. Not shrinks. Not fades. Reverses — the two sides swap sign.
How far? To roughly plus thirty milli volts. So the swing is about minus seventy to plus thirty. Notice it does not stop at zero — it overshoots straight past neutral.
Read the curve. Flat at rest. A nudge up to threshold. Then the near-vertical climb as sodium floods in, past zero to the peak. That climb is depolarisation.
And state the definition exactly: this reversed state is the action potential. Not the stimulus, not the whole graph — the reversed state itself.
Now hold the logic, because it makes this reconstructible under pressure rather than memorisable. Only a cation moving inward can make the inside positive. Positive charge must physically enter.
And the membrane was already holding sodium outside, at high concentration. So the cation is sodium, the direction inward, and once the gates open the gradient does the rest for free.
String loaded है। अब कोई pluck करता है। जो stimulus threshold तक पहुँचता है वो उस site पर rapid, self regenerating voltage change trigger करता है — और फ़िलहाल सिर्फ़ उसी site पर।
जो बदलता है वो permeability है। Stimulated point पर membrane अचानक sodium के लिए कहीं ज़्यादा permeable हो जाती है। यही switch दबता है। उसके बाद सब नतीजा है।
क्योंकि याद कीजिए बाहर क्या था। Sodium, मात्रा में, एक membrane से रोका हुआ जो उसे मुश्किल से आने देती थी, और negative interior से खिंचता हुआ। Gate खोलिए और sodium अंदर टूट पड़ता है।
अंदर आता है, positive charge लेकर, जब तक अंदर positive और बाहर negative न हो जाए। Polarity reverse होती है। घटती नहीं। मिटती नहीं। Reverse होती है — दोनों sides का चिह्न बदलता है।
कितना? लगभग plus तीस milli volts तक। तो swing है लगभग minus सत्तर से plus तीस। ध्यान दीजिए ये zero पर रुकता नहीं। ये neutral पार करके positive में चला जाता है।
Curve पढ़िए। Rest पर सपाट। Threshold तक हल्का उठाव। फिर लगभग सीधी चढ़ाई, जैसे sodium अंदर भरता है, zero के पार peak तक। यही चढ़ाई depolarisation है।
और definition बिलकुल ठीक बोलिए: यही reversed state action potential है। न stimulus, न पूरा graph — वो reversed state खुद।
अब logic पकड़िए, क्योंकि यही इसे pressure में दोबारा बना पाने लायक़ बनाता है, रटने लायक़ नहीं। अंदर को positive सिर्फ़ वो cation बना सकता है जो अंदर आए। Positive charge को घुसना ही होगा।
और membrane पहले से sodium को बाहर, high concentration में, तैयार रखे थी। तो cation है sodium, direction inward, और gates खुलते ही बाक़ी काम gradient मुफ़्त में कर देता है।

board_events.text: BRIEF OVERSHOOT (hyperpolarisation): continued K+ efflux can make the inside MORE negative than rest, for an instant.
RESTORATION: the Na-K pump quietly resets the ion concentrations, readying the site for the next impulse.
The REFRACTORY PERIOD is why impulses don't run backwards.
Phase-tag every ion: Na+ IN = depolarisation. K+ OUT = repolarisation.
Same curve, four logical steps. Learn the sequence, not just the shape.

segments.text: The inside has gone positive. If it stayed there the neuron could never fire again. So the flip must be undone, quickly. That is steps two, three and four.
Step two, repolarisation. Almost immediately the sodium gates shut and the potassium gates open. Two things at once: the inward door closes, an outward door opens.
And potassium, concentrated inside, now moves out. Positive charge leaves, the inside goes negative again, and resting polarity is restored. That is what repolarisation literally says.
Look at the same curve, but read the falling limb. The peak, then the drop back through zero, down towards rest — that whole descent is potassium leaving.

Step three, the brief overshoot, or hyperpolarisation. Potassium efflux does not stop the instant rest is reached — it continues, and can briefly make the inside more negative than rest. Find the small dip below the resting line.
Step four, restoration. The sodium potassium pump quietly resets the ion concentrations for the next impulse — no spike, just the pump doing the accounting afterwards.
And your book attaches a consequence: the refractory period — the brief window when the site cannot fire again — is why impulses do not run backwards. The patch behind is momentarily unresponsive.
Now the discipline that saves marks. Phase-tag every ion. Sodium in equals depolarisation. Potassium out equals repolarisation. Never say a nerve ion without saying its phase in the same breath.
Same curve as the last section, four logical steps, and each step is a different question. Learn the sequence, not just the shape.
अंदर positive हो चुका है। अगर वहीं रह गया, neuron बेकार है — दोबारा fire नहीं कर पाएगा। तो flip undo करना ही होगा, जल्दी। यही steps दो, तीन और चार हैं।
Step दो, repolarisation। लगभग तुरंत sodium gates बंद और potassium gates खुल जाते हैं। दो चीज़ें एक साथ: अंदर का दरवाज़ा बंद, बाहर का खुला।
और potassium, जो अंदर concentrated है, अब बाहर निकलता है। Positive charge चला जाता है। अंदर फिर negative, resting polarity वापस। Repolarisation शब्द यही कहता है: दोबारा polarise होना।
वही curve देखिए, पर गिरता हिस्सा पढ़िए। Peak, फिर zero के पार नीचे, rest की तरफ़ — ये पूरा उतार potassium के निकलने का है।

Step तीन, brief overshoot, या hyperpolarisation। Potassium efflux rest पर पहुँचते ही रुकता नहीं — चलता रहता है, और एक पल को अंदर को rest से भी ज़्यादा negative बना सकता है। Resting line के नीचे वो छोटा dip ढूँढिए।
Step चार, restoration। Sodium potassium pump चुपचाप ion concentrations reset करता है, site को अगले impulse के लिए तैयार करता है। चुपचाप सही शब्द है — कोई spike नहीं, बस pump बाद में हिसाब करता हुआ।
और book एक नतीजा जोड़ती है: refractory period — वो छोटी खिड़की जब site दोबारा fire नहीं कर सकती — इसी से impulses पीछे नहीं दौड़ते। पीछे वाला patch पल भर बेअसर है, तो रास्ता सिर्फ़ आगे।
अब वो discipline जो marks बचाती है। हर ion को phase से tag कीजिए। Sodium in यानी depolarisation। Potassium out यानी repolarisation। Nerve का कोई ion बिना phase बोले मत बोलिए।
क्योंकि देखिए हमने क्या किया — पिछले section वाला वही curve, चार logical steps, और हर step अलग question है। Sequence सीखिए, सिर्फ़ shape नहीं।

sections.title: Propagation: how the impulse marches forward

board_events.text: Propagation along the axon
The reversed, depolarised point acts as the STIMULUS for the patch just ahead of it.
That patch depolarises next. And that one stimulates the next. And so on.

board_events.text: So the impulse marches forward, REGENERATING AT FULL STRENGTH at every step.
This is the domino logic. The impulse never fades with distance.
Behind the wave, the Na-K pump re-loads the membrane, readying it for the next message.
Nothing has travelled the length of the axon. A disturbance has been recreated, step after step.

segments.text: We have a full action potential at one spot. But an impulse that stays there is not a message. It has to reach the other end. So how does it move?

Here is the mechanism, and it is beautifully economical. The reversed, depolarised point acts as the stimulus for the patch of membrane just ahead of it. The flip becomes the trigger for the next flip.
So that patch depolarises next. And once reversed, it becomes the stimulus for the patch ahead. And that one for the next. The impulse is its own cause, over and over, down the axon.
Watch the three steps. A reversed patch near the start, everything ahead still polarised. Then the reversal has moved one patch along, and behind it the membrane is already re-loading. Then again.
And the crucial consequence: the impulse marches forward, regenerating at full strength at every step. Not weakening. Not spreading out. Rebuilt, fresh, at full size, each time.
That is the domino logic from earlier, now with its machinery filled in. And it explains something remarkable — the impulse never fades with distance. The last centimetre is as strong as the first.
Meanwhile, behind the wave, the sodium potassium pump re-loads the membrane for the next message. The wave passes, and the string is restrung behind it, ready to be plucked again.
So look at what happened. Nothing travelled the length of the axon. A disturbance was recreated, step after step. The message arrives, but nothing was ever sent.
एक जगह पूरा action potential बन चुका है। पर जो impulse एक जगह पड़ा रहे वो message नहीं। उसे दूसरे सिरे तक जाना है। तो चलता कैसे है?
ये रहा mechanism, और ये बेहद economical है। वो reversed, depolarised point अपने आगे वाले membrane patch के लिए stimulus बन जाता है। Flip खुद अगले flip का trigger बन जाता है।
तो अगला patch depolarise होता है। और reverse होते ही वो अपने आगे वाले के लिए stimulus बन जाता है। और वो अगले के लिए। Impulse अपनी ही वजह है, बार-बार, पूरे axon पर।
तीनों steps देखिए। शुरू के पास एक reversed patch, आगे सब polarised। फिर reversal एक patch आगे खिसका, और पीछे membrane पहले ही re-load हो रही है। फिर वही।
और अहम नतीजा: impulse आगे बढ़ता है, हर step पर full strength पर regenerate होते हुए। कमज़ोर नहीं होता। फैलता नहीं। हर बार नए सिरे से, पूरे size में।
यही पहले वाली domino logic है, अब machinery के साथ। और इससे एक remarkable बात निकलती है — impulse distance के साथ fade नहीं होता। आख़िरी centimetre पहले जितना strong है।
इस बीच, wave के पीछे, sodium potassium pump membrane को अगले message के लिए re-load करता है। Wave गुज़रती है, और पीछे string फिर चढ़ जाती है, दोबारा pluck होने को तैयार।
तो देखिए हुआ क्या। Axon की लंबाई पर कुछ travel नहीं किया। एक भी ion ने वो सफ़र नहीं किया। एक disturbance बार-बार recreate हुई। Message पहुँच गया, पर भेजा कुछ नहीं गया।

sections.title: Continuous vs saltatory conduction

board_events.text: Conduction speed — continuous vs saltatory
UNMYELINATED FIBRE: the impulse regenerates at EVERY point along the membrane.
That is CONTINUOUS conduction — and it is relatively SLOW.
MYELINATED FIBRE: myelin insulates the axon, so depolarisation can only happen at the exposed NODES OF RANVIER.
The impulse therefore JUMPS from node to node — SALTATORY conduction.

board_events.text: saltare = 'to leap'. Saltatory is much FASTER and more energy-efficient.
Do not swap them. Continuous is the slow, unmyelinated mode. Saltatory is the fast, myelinated mode.

segments.text: Now we cash in the myelin distinction — because myelin is why two fibres carrying the same impulse can differ enormously in speed.
Take the unmyelinated fibre first. No insulation, so the membrane is exposed everywhere. Which means the impulse regenerates at every point along the membrane. Every single point, in sequence.
That is continuous conduction, and here is the thing — it is relatively slow. Not because any one step is slow, but because there are so many steps. Regenerating everywhere means stopping everywhere.
Now the myelinated fibre. Myelin insulates the axon, and insulated membrane cannot depolarise. So depolarisation happens only where the membrane is exposed — exactly at the nodes of Ranvier.

So the impulse cannot regenerate in between. It jumps from node to node. That jumping is saltatory conduction. All those nodes we labelled now have a purpose — they are the only places the impulse can land.
Compare the pictures. Above, a chain of tiny regeneration points, one after another, all the way. Below, three big arcs leaping between nodes. Same distance, far fewer stops.

<excited> The word tells you the mechanism — saltare is Latin for to leap. Skipping the insulated stretches makes saltatory conduction much faster, and more energy efficient, because far fewer patches need pumping back afterwards.
So lock the pairing, because it is swapped constantly: continuous is the slow, unmyelinated mode. Saltatory is the fast, myelinated mode. Say it in that order, both halves together, every time.
अब myelin वाली distinction का फ़ायदा — क्योंकि myelin ही वजह है कि एक ही impulse ले जाती दो fibres की speed में ज़मीन-आसमान का फ़र्क़ हो।
पहले unmyelinated fibre। कोई insulation नहीं, तो membrane हर जगह exposed। मतलब impulse membrane के हर point पर regenerate होता है। एक-एक point पर, sequence में।
यही continuous conduction है, और बात ये है — ये relatively slow है। इसलिए नहीं कि कोई step धीमा है, बल्कि इसलिए कि steps बहुत हैं। हर जगह regenerate मतलब हर जगह रुकना।
अब myelinated fibre। Myelin axon को insulate करता है, और insulated membrane depolarise नहीं हो सकती। तो depolarisation सिर्फ़ वहाँ जहाँ membrane exposed है — ठीक nodes of Ranvier पर।
तो impulse बीच में regenerate कर ही नहीं सकता। वो node से node कूदता है। यही saltatory conduction है। जिन nodes को label किया था उनका मक़सद अब साफ़ — impulse सिर्फ़ वहीं उतर सकता है।
Pictures compare कीजिए। ऊपर, छोटे regeneration points की लड़ी, एक के बाद एक। नीचे, nodes के बीच तीन बड़े arcs। वही distance, कहीं कम रुकावटें।

<excited> शब्द mechanism बता रहा है — saltare Latin में मतलब कूदना। Insulated हिस्से छोड़ देने से saltatory conduction कहीं तेज़ हो जाती है, और energy efficient भी, क्योंकि बाद में कम patches pump करने पड़ते हैं।
तो जोड़ी lock कीजिए, क्योंकि यही सबसे swap होती है: continuous यानी slow, unmyelinated mode। Saltatory यानी fast, myelinated mode। हर बार इसी order में, दोनों हिस्से साथ।

sections.title: The synapse: electrical vs chemical

board_events.text: The synapse — the junction where a signal is handed on
A SYNAPSE is the junction at which one neuron passes a signal to the next cell.
ELECTRICAL SYNAPSE: pre- and post-synaptic membranes lie extremely close, about 5 nm.
Current flows DIRECTLY across. Transmission is very fast, and resembles conduction along a single axon. RARE in humans.
CHEMICAL SYNAPSE: the membranes are separated by a fluid-filled SYNAPTIC CLEFT, about 10-20 nm, bridged by chemicals.

board_events.text: Closer gap = faster. Wider gap = needs a chemical courier.
The chemical step is slower — but it is exactly what makes transmission UNIDIRECTIONAL.

segments.text: The impulse has reached the end of the axon. Now the last problem: this neuron is not the destination. And the two cells are not continuous — there is a junction.
That junction has a name. A synapse is the junction at which one neuron passes a signal to the next cell. Your book gives two kinds, distinguished by one physical fact: how wide the gap is.
First, the electrical synapse. Here the pre synaptic and post synaptic membranes lie extremely close — about five nanometres apart. Almost touching.

And because they are that close, current flows directly across. No middleman. Transmission is very fast, and your book says it resembles conduction along a single axon. But note: electrical synapses are rare in humans.
Second, the chemical synapse. The membranes are separated by a fluid filled synaptic cleft, about ten to twenty nanometres wide. Too wide for current to jump — so the gap is bridged by chemicals.
Put them side by side. A hair-thin gap with current flowing straight over. Versus a wider gap with molecules ferrying across. Two solutions to the same problem, chosen by geometry.
So the principle: a closer gap means faster, direct transmission. A wider gap means you need a chemical courier. The anatomy dictates the mechanism.

<curious> But why would the body choose the slower option — and use it almost everywhere? Because the chemical step is not a workaround. It is exactly what makes transmission unidirectional. And that is worth paying for.
Impulse axon के सिरे तक पहुँच गया। अब आख़िरी problem: ये neuron मंज़िल नहीं। Message को अगली cell तक जाना है। और दोनों cells continuous नहीं — बीच में junction है।
उस junction का नाम है। Synapse वो junction है जिस पर एक neuron signal अगली cell को pass करता है। Book दो तरह के बताती है, फ़र्क़ एक physical fact से: gap कितना चौड़ा है।
पहला, electrical synapse। यहाँ pre synaptic और post synaptic membranes बेहद पास हैं — लगभग पाँच nanometre की दूरी। छूने जैसी।
और इतने पास होने से current सीधा आर-पार बहता है। कोई बिचौलिया नहीं। Transmission बहुत तेज़, और book कहती है ये एक ही axon पर conduction जैसी लगती है। पर नोट: electrical synapses humans में rare हैं।

दूसरा, chemical synapse। Membranes के बीच fluid से भरा gap है जिसे synaptic cleft कहते हैं, लगभग दस से बीस nanometre चौड़ा। कई गुना ज़्यादा — इतना कि current कूद न सके। तो gap chemicals से पाटा जाता है।
दोनों साथ रखिए। एक बाल जितना पतला gap, current सीधा बहता हुआ। बनाम चौड़ा gap, molecules नाव की तरह पार जाते हुए। एक problem के दो solutions, geometry से चुने।
तो principle: पास वाला gap यानी तेज़, direct transmission। चौड़ा gap यानी chemical courier चाहिए। Anatomy ही mechanism तय करती है।
<curious> पर body धीमा option चुनेगी क्यों — और लगभग हर जगह इस्तेमाल क्यों करेगी? क्योंकि chemical step जुगाड़ नहीं है। यही transmission को unidirectional बनाता है। और वो क़ीमत चुकाने लायक़ है।

sections.title: Across the chemical synapse, step by step

board_events.text: Transmission across a chemical synapse
Step 1: the impulse reaches the AXON TERMINAL.
Step 2: Ca2+ enters the terminal.
Step 3: SYNAPTIC VESICLES fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release a NEUROTRANSMITTER (e.g. acetylcholine) into the cleft.
Step 4: it binds RECEPTORS on the postsynaptic membrane.
Step 5: ion channels open. A new potential develops — EXCITATORY (EPSP) or INHIBITORY (IPSP).

board_events.text: Cause precedes effect: impulse → Ca2+ in → release → binding. Any other order is a distractor.
Only one side has vesicles; only the other has receptors. THAT is why transmission is unidirectional.

segments.text: This sequence is examined as a sequence — scrambled orders are the standard distractor. Learn it as a chain of causes, not a list.
Step one: the impulse reaches the axon terminal. Everything downstream is triggered by that arrival.
Step two: calcium enters the terminal. Note the ion — calcium, not sodium and not potassium. Those two ran the action potential. Calcium runs the handover. Different job, different ion.
Step three: synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release a neurotransmitter into the cleft — your book's example is acetylcholine. Calcium is the signal to dock and dump.
Step four: it crosses the cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. The message has now changed form twice — electrical to chemical, and about to become electrical again.
Step five: that binding opens ion channels, and a new potential develops. And it comes in two flavours — excitatory, an E P S P, or inhibitory, an I P S P.
Trace it once: impulse in, calcium through the membrane, vesicles fusing, transmitter crossing the cleft, receptors on the far side, channels opening, E P S P or I P S P.

Now the discipline. Cause precedes effect. Impulse, then calcium in, then release, then binding. If an option releases transmitter before the impulse arrives, or moves calcium out, reject it on causal grounds alone.

And the answer to the question we left hanging. Only the presynaptic side has vesicles; only the postsynaptic side has receptors. Speakers on one side, ears on the other. That is why transmission is unidirectional.
ये sequence यहाँ लगभग सबसे ज़्यादा exam में आता है, और sequence की तरह ही — उल्टा order standard distractor है। इसे causes की chain की तरह सीखिए, list की तरह नहीं।
Step एक: impulse axon terminal तक पहुँचता है। पूरा axon तय करके, हर जगह regenerate होते हुए, अब knob पर। आगे का सब इसी पहुँचने से trigger होता है।
Step दो: calcium terminal में enter करता है। Ion नोट कीजिए — calcium, न sodium न potassium। वो दोनों action potential चला रहे थे। Calcium handover चलाता है। अलग काम, अलग ion।

Step तीन: synaptic vesicles presynaptic membrane से fuse होकर cleft में neurotransmitter release करती हैं। Book का example acetylcholine। Vesicles loaded बैठी थीं; calcium वो signal है — dock करो और उड़ेल दो।
Step चार: neurotransmitter cleft पार करके postsynaptic membrane के receptors से bind होता है। Message दो बार रूप बदल चुका — electrical से chemical, और अब दोबारा electrical बनने वाला।
Step पाँच: वो binding ion channels खोलती है, और एक नया potential बनता है। और वो दो flavours में — excitatory, यानी E P S P, या inhibitory, यानी I P S P।
एक बार trace कीजिए: impulse अंदर, calcium membrane से नीचे, vesicles fuse होतीं, transmitter पीले cleft को पार करता, दूसरी तरफ़ receptors, channels खुलते, E P S P या I P S P।

अब discipline। कारण पहले, नतीजा बाद में। Impulse, फिर calcium अंदर, फिर release, फिर binding। कोई option impulse से पहले transmitter release करे, या calcium बाहर ले जाए, तो सिर्फ़ causal ground पर reject कीजिए।
और उस सवाल का जवाब जो अधूरा था। Vesicles सिर्फ़ presynaptic side पर; receptors सिर्फ़ postsynaptic side पर। एक तरफ़ speakers, दूसरी तरफ़ कान। इसीलिए transmission unidirectional है।

sections.title: EPSP, IPSP, and the net decision

board_events.text: Whether the next neuron fires is NOT decided by a single message
One arriving signal does not command the next cell. It only gets a say.
A given neuron receives MANY inputs at once — some excitatory, some inhibitory.
It is the NET EFFECT of all of them on the postsynaptic membrane that determines whether the threshold is crossed.
An EPSP nudges the membrane TOWARDS firing.
An IPSP pulls it AWAY from firing.

board_events.text: This is the cellular basis of the 'decision-making' the nervous system performs at every junction.
So a synapse is not a relay that simply repeats. It is a place where a vote is counted.

segments.text: One more idea before the worked examples — the one that turns this from wiring into biology.
Whether the postsynaptic neuron fires its own impulse is not decided by a single message. One arriving signal does not command the next cell. It only gets a say.
Because a neuron receives many inputs at once — some excitatory, some inhibitory, arriving together on the same membrane. It is listening to a crowd, not one voice.
And it is the net effect of all of them that determines whether threshold is crossed. Add up everything arriving, and ask one question: did the sum reach threshold?
The two directions are simple. An E P S P, an excitatory postsynaptic potential, nudges the membrane towards firing. It pushes the voltage up, closer to threshold.
An I P S P, an inhibitory postsynaptic potential, does the opposite — it pulls the membrane away from firing, further from threshold. One says go; one says wait.

Look at the picture. Three excitatory inputs and one inhibitory, on the same cell. On the right the running total wobbles as they arrive — and only when enough agree does it cross the dashed line and fire.
Your book gives this its proper weight, and so should you: this is the cellular basis of the decision making the nervous system performs at every junction.
So revise your picture of a synapse. It is not a relay that repeats what it was told. It is a place where a vote is counted.
Worked examples से पहले एक और idea — वही जो इसे wiring से biology बनाता है।
Postsynaptic neuron अपना impulse fire करेगा या नहीं, ये एक message से तय नहीं होता। एक आता signal अगली cell को हुक्म नहीं देता। उसे बस अपनी बात रखने का मौक़ा मिलता है।
क्योंकि neuron पर एक साथ कई inputs आते हैं — कुछ excitatory, कुछ inhibitory, सब एक ही membrane पर। वो एक आवाज़ नहीं सुन रहा। वो भीड़ सुन रहा है।
और उन सबका net effect तय करता है कि threshold cross हुआ या नहीं। जो आ रहा है सब जोड़िए, और एक सवाल: क्या जोड़ threshold तक पहुँचा?
दोनों directions simple हैं। E P S P, यानी excitatory postsynaptic potential, membrane को firing की तरफ़ धकेलता है। Voltage ऊपर, threshold के क़रीब।
I P S P, यानी inhibitory postsynaptic potential, उल्टा करता है — membrane को firing से दूर खींचता है, threshold से और परे। एक कहता है चलो; दूसरा कहता है रुको।
Picture देखिए। तीन excitatory inputs और एक inhibitory, एक ही cell पर। दाईं तरफ़ running total डोलता है — और सिर्फ़ तब, जब काफ़ी सारे सहमत हों, वो dashed line पार करके fire करता है।
Book इसे पूरी अहमियत देती है, आपको भी देनी चाहिए: यही उस decision making का cellular basis है जो nervous system हर junction पर करता है। Decision making, एक cell के level पर।
तो synapse की picture बदलिए। ये relay नहीं जो सुनी बात दोहरा दे। ये वो जगह है जहाँ vote गिने जाते हैं। और आपने जो भी सोचा है, वो तह में उन्हीं votes की बहुत बड़ी गिनती था।

board_events.text: The defining clue: 'present in cyton and dendrites, absent in axon'.
That is the textbook signature of NISSL'S GRANULES.
Chemical nature: aggregations of ROUGH ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM, with ribosomes.
Function: PROTEIN SYNTHESIS for the neuron.
Common slip: naming 'mitochondria'. But mitochondria occur in the axon too — they fail the 'absent in axon' test.

segments.text: First worked example, a C B S E board question — a diagram identification. Read it and notice how it is built.
In a labelled diagram of a neuron, structure P is found only in the cyton and dendrites, but never in the axon. Name P, state its chemical nature, and its function. Three marks, three asks.
Look at the figure. Granules in the dendrites. Granules in the cell body. And along the whole axon — nothing, crossed out.

Now find the defining clue. It is the phrase present in cyton and dendrites, absent in axon. That is not a hint. That is a fingerprint — you have been handed the distribution and asked to name the owner.
And that distribution is the textbook signature of Nissl's granules. Nothing else in the neuron has exactly that pattern. So P is Nissl's granules, and the first mark is banked.
Second ask: chemical nature. Aggregations of rough endoplasmic reticulum, carrying ribosomes. Say rough — smooth E R would be wrong, and the word is doing real work.
Third ask: function. Protein synthesis for the neuron. And notice you did not memorise that separately — ribosomes make proteins, so the function follows from the chemical nature you just stated.

Now the slip your book flags, because it catches good students. Many write mitochondria — sensible, until you test it against the clue. Mitochondria occur in the axon too. They fail the absent in axon test.
पहला worked example, C B S E board question — diagram identification। पढ़िए और देखिए ये बना कैसे है।
Neuron के labelled diagram में structure P सिर्फ़ cyton और dendrites में मिलता है, axon में कभी नहीं। P का नाम, chemical nature, और function बताइए। तीन marks, तीन माँगें।
Figure देखिए। Dendrites में granules। Cell body में granules। और पूरे axon पर — कुछ नहीं, cross लगा।
अब defining clue ढूँढिए। वो phrase — cyton और dendrites में present, axon में absent। ये hint नहीं। ये fingerprint है — आपको distribution थमा दी गई और मालिक का नाम पूछा गया।
और वो distribution Nissl's granules का textbook signature है। Neuron में और किसी का बिलकुल यही pattern नहीं। तो P है Nissl's granules, पहला mark pakka।
दूसरी माँग: chemical nature। Rough endoplasmic reticulum के aggregations, जिन पर ribosomes हैं। Rough बोलिए — smooth E R गलत होगा, और शब्द असल में काम कर रहा है।
तीसरी माँग: function। Neuron के लिए protein synthesis। और ध्यान दीजिए, ये अलग से रटा नहीं — ribosomes protein बनाते हैं, तो function उसी chemical nature से निकल आया।

अब वो slip जिसे book flag करती है, क्योंकि ये अच्छे students को पकड़ती है। कई mitochondria लिख देते हैं — समझदार guess, जब तक clue पर test न करें। Mitochondria axon में भी होते हैं। वो absent in axon वाला test fail करते हैं, और question उसी पर बना था।

During the DEPOLARISATION phase of an action potential, the axonal membrane becomes most permeable to which ion, and in which direction does it move?

board_events.text: Depolarisation = polarity reversal = the inside turning positive.
The only way the inside turns positive is by an INFLUX OF A CATION.
The resting membrane was holding Na+ out. Open the gates and Na+ floods in. Answer: (b).
Quick elimination: K+ moving out (a) is repolarisation, not depolarisation. (c) and (d) don't fit the reversal logic at all.
SPEED TRAP: students who memorise 'K+ for nerves' without phase-tagging pick (a).

segments.text: Second example, N E E T style, and the real skill is speed — this is a question you should reconstruct rather than recall.
During the depolarisation phase of an action potential, the axonal membrane becomes most permeable to which ion, and in which direction does it move?
The options: (a) potassium, outward. (b) sodium, inward. (c) calcium, outward. (d) chloride, inward. Only one combination survives the logic.
Follow the chain on the left of the figure. Three links, and you can walk them in about five seconds once you have done it a few times.
Link one: depolarisation means polarity reversal, which means the inside turning positive. Start from the definition, always.
Link two: the only way the inside turns positive is by an influx of a cation. That instantly kills both outward options — you have halved the paper's options without recalling a fact.
Link three: which cation? The resting membrane was holding sodium out, at high concentration, against its gradient. Open the gates and sodium floods in. So the answer is (b), sodium, inward.
Now the eliminations. Potassium moving out — option (a) — is real, but it is repolarisation. Right ion, wrong phase. And (c) and (d) do not fit the reversal logic at all.

<whisper> And that is the speed trap. Students who memorised potassium for nerves, without phase tagging, see a familiar ion and pick (a). The option is not wrong because it is nonsense. It is wrong because it belongs to the next phase.
दूसरा example, N E E T style, और असली skill speed है — इसे याद करने के बजाय दोबारा बना लेना चाहिए।
Action potential के depolarisation phase में axonal membrane किस ion के लिए सबसे ज़्यादा permeable होती है, और वो किस direction में move करता है?
Options: (a) potassium, outward। (b) sodium, inward। (c) calcium, outward। (d) chloride, inward। चार ions, दो directions — logic से सिर्फ़ एक combination बचता है।
Figure के बाईं तरफ़ वाली chain follow कीजिए। तीन कड़ियाँ, और कुछ practice के बाद आप इन्हें लगभग पाँच seconds में चल जाएँगे।
कड़ी एक: depolarisation मतलब polarity reversal, यानी अंदर का positive होना। हमेशा definition से शुरू।
कड़ी दो: अंदर positive सिर्फ़ तब जब cation अंदर आए। Positive charge को आना ही होगा। इससे दोनों outward options तुरंत मर जाते हैं — बिना एक fact याद किए आपने options आधे कर दिए।
कड़ी तीन: कौन-सा cation? Resting membrane sodium को बाहर रोके थी, high concentration में, gradient के ख़िलाफ़। Gates खोलिए और sodium अंदर भर जाता है। तो answer है (b), sodium, inward।
अब eliminations। Potassium का बाहर जाना — option (a) — असली event है, पर वो repolarisation है, depolarisation नहीं। Ion सही, phase गलत। और (c) और (d) reversal logic में बैठते ही नहीं।
<whisper> और यही speed trap है। जिन्होंने बिना phase tag किए potassium for nerves रट लिया, वो जाना-पहचाना ion देखकर (a) चुन लेते हैं। Option इसलिए गलत नहीं कि बेतुका है। इसलिए कि वो अगले phase का है।

board_events.text: Multipolar — one axon plus many dendrites — dominates the cerebral cortex. So C-2.
Bipolar — one axon plus one dendrite — is the classic retinal neuron. So B-1.
Unipolar is described as occurring usually in the embryonic stage. So A-3.
Answer: A-3, B-1, C-2. Work from the pair you are surest of, then eliminate.

segments.text: Third example, C U E T style — a match the column on neuron types. These look like pure recall, but a technique makes them nearly free.
Column one gives the types: A, unipolar. B, bipolar. C, multipolar. Column two gives locations: one, retina of the eye. Two, cerebral cortex. Three, embryonic stage.
Here is the technique. Do not start at A and grind down. Start with the pair you are surest of, commit it, and let elimination shrink the problem.
For most students that anchor is multipolar. One axon plus many dendrites, and it dominates the cerebral cortex. So C goes to two. One pairing down, and the board is smaller.
Next, bipolar. One axon plus one dendrite — the classic retinal neuron, the example every book uses. So B goes to one.

Which leaves unipolar and the embryonic stage. And note: even if you had forgotten it, elimination just handed it to you free. But it is independently true — your book says unipolar occurs usually in the embryonic stage. So A goes to three.
The full answer: A three, B one, C two. Write it in the order the question asks, not the order you solved it in — a silly place to lose a mark.
And carry the method, not the answer. Work from the pair you are surest of, then eliminate. In a match the column you are never asked to know everything — only enough to corner the rest.
तीसरा example, C U E T style — neuron types पर match the column। ये pure recall लगते हैं, पर एक technique इन्हें लगभग मुफ़्त बना देती है।
Column एक types देता है: A, unipolar। B, bipolar। C, multipolar। Column दो locations: एक, retina of the eye। दो, cerebral cortex। तीन, embryonic stage।
ये रही technique। A से शुरू करके रगड़ते मत जाइए। जिस pair पर सबसे भरोसा है उससे शुरू कीजिए, उसे pakka कीजिए, और elimination को problem छोटी करने दीजिए।
ज़्यादातर के लिए वो anchor multipolar है। एक axon plus कई dendrites, और यही cerebral cortex में छाया है। तो C जाएगा दो के साथ। एक pairing हुई, board छोटा हुआ।
अगला, bipolar। एक axon plus एक dendrite — classic retinal neuron, वही example जो हर book देती है। तो B जाएगा एक के साथ।

अब बचे unipolar और embryonic stage। और notice: अगर भूल भी गए होते, elimination ने ये मुफ़्त थमा दिया। पर ये अपने आप में भी सही है — book कहती है unipolar usually embryonic stage में होते हैं। तो A जाएगा तीन के साथ।
पूरा answer: A तीन, B एक, C दो। जिस order में question माँगे उसी में लिखिए, उसमें नहीं जिसमें हल किया — mark गँवाने की बेवक़ूफ़ जगह।
और method ले जाइए, answer नहीं। सबसे पक्के pair से शुरू, फिर eliminate। Match the column में सब कुछ जानने को नहीं कहा जाता — बस इतना कि बाक़ी को घेर सकें।

sections.title: Assertion-Reason: why myelin is faster

board_events.text: Example 4 — NEET high-difficulty: assertion-reason
Assertion (A): Conduction of a nerve impulse is faster in a myelinated neuron than in a non-myelinated one.
Reason (R): In a myelinated fibre, the impulse is regenerated continuously at every point of the membrane.
(a) Both true, R explains A   (b) Both true, R does not explain A   (c) A true, R false   (d) A false, R true

board_events.caption: Testing each statement separately, then the link
